brief_context: The Domestic Council representing 16 women's organisations in this country.
brief_extract:
It also provides instruction for electrical housecraft advisors and domestic science teachers. Netherlands Domestic Council
The Netherlands Domestic Council has representatives from 16 women's organisations, and its aim is to promote efficient housekeeping and look after the consumer's interests. Contracts are made regularly by written enquiry with 5,000 housewives, who are divided into panels according to status, family size and residence in town or country.

brief_context: Location of the Building Centre visited by Miss Duffield.

The Council publishes booklets on such equipment as washers and refrigerators, and takes an active part in promoting care labelling and the provision of adequate instruction regarding the washing of different fabrics. Building Centre, Rotterdam
The information gained at the Domestic Council stood Miss Duffield in good stead when she visited the internationally known Building Centre. Founded at a time when much rebuilding was necessary, its aim was to promote better standards with the limited means available.

First underground mains cable, Birmingham 1890

Romance Under Our Feet —some highlights of cable history

IF electricity is the life blood of our industrial society, cables and wires and transmission lines are its arteries. Without them there would be no power and no communications.

brief_context: Country requiring vast quantities of cable for large projects.
article_title: Romance Under Our Feet —some highlights of cable history
brief_extract: From every power station a network of cables and lines radiates over the countryside to form part of the familiar grid system. The modernisation of the mines and the electrification of the railways are but two of the many large projects in the UK requiring vast quantities of cable and wire for the transmission of power. Factories, ships, aircraft, as well as homes throughout the country would be lifeless shells without the wiring which brings power, heat and light.

brief_extract: Tom Callender, son of the company's founder, concentrated his interest on electrical work and was greatly impressed by the illumination in the St. Petersburg Opera House in 1880 provided by the new Jablochkoff candles, which were to be seen three years later at Covent Garden Opera House when Callender's installed the underground mains. Later he sailed home from the USA on the first large liner to have an effective electrical installation and the contrast with the paraffin lamps in the ship on which he made the outward journey confirmed his intentions to concentrate on electrical development.

brief_context: Refers to annual plants originating from South Africa.
brief_extract: Annuals can be used to form complete borders and make a most colourful contribution to the garden, or they can furnish any odd spot in the garden providing it is not in the shade of trees or buildings. I am particularly fond of the South African annuals of which dimorphtheca the Star of the Veldt, is one of the brightest; it grows to about one foot high and has bright star-like flowers in a wide range of attractive colours. In addition to the ones already mentioned there are such treasures as eschscholtzias, anchusas, candytuft, clarkias, saponaria, sweet sultan, scabious, viscaria, and love in a mist, to say nothing of the finest of all annuals the sweet pea.

brief_context: Region where trained archaeologists are relatively few.
brief_extract:
But the fact of the matter is that the ‘archaeological establishment’ in this country is simply not geared to cope with this great upsurge of interest in what after all is a fairly recondite subject. In Scotland trained archaeologists are relatively few on the ground and the majority, being tied to jobs, cannot be expected to cope with the popular demands on their time and energies. All this constitutes part of the Problem of Leisure — a problem created by the fact that
science has now made it possible for large numbers of people to pursue humanistic and aesthetic studies which in turn are inadequately equipped to cope with the demands made on them.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the tombs of the Pharaohs seen on TV.
brief_extract: Having brought up a family they have neglected their reading, forgotten their youthful enthusiasm and then suddenly in middle age felt that they were missing something. Television shows them the marvels of the tombs of the Egyptian Pharaohs — the fascination of the extraordinary palaces of Crete and Mycenae — the mysteries of Stonehenge and New Grange. No wonder then that they rush to enrol in any available archaeology study group.

Caroline Haslett was a woman of many parts, and in this biography those who knew her will realise once again the warmth of her nature and the strength of purpose which were so characteristic of her.

brief_context: Location of Caroline Haslett's childhood village.
brief_extract: There must be a vast number of parents whose hesitant 'I have a daughter' caused Caroline to make her well-known reply 'we must do something about it', and this 'something' opened 'doors of opportunity' to countless girls. She believed that electricity was the emancipator of women from domestic drudgery, which in the Sussex village of her childhood she had seen sapping the energies of many girls and women. She hated waste of any kind, and most of all of human potentialities.

brief_context: Period context for finding alumen salt in volcanic caves.
brief_extract:
Aluminium
Although the use of aluminium for cooking utensils became widely used only after the first World War, the first recorded use of aluminium for domestic purposes occurred soon after 1854 when aluminium knife and fork handles were made for Napoleon III for a banquet. The word itself is derived from alumen, the name of a salt found in volcanic caves in Roman times. Aluminium has the advantage of being relatively cheap, light, malleable and unchippable, therefore, it is comparatively easy and economical to work.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the reach of contractors and inspecting engineers.
article_title: Quality and Reliability Year and the NICEIC
brief_extract: Perhaps the tradition of voluntary cooperation works better here; certainly the idea that an electrical contractor should voluntarily bind himself to abide by certain rules really is to his credit and of real worth. In its ten years of existence the NICEIC has steadily grown and now there are no fewer than 6,400 names and addresses in the latest edition of the Roll to whom the consumer can apply for electrical work to be done - there is an Approved Electrical Contractor within the reach of everyone in the United Kingdom. Just as those whose names appear in the Roll are obliged to abide by certain standards, it is surely too the citizen's obligation to support the work of the Council and so contribute towards maintaining a high standard of electrical installation work.

brief_context: Location from which applications for 'Contractor's Handbook' were received.
article_title: Quality and Reliability Year and the NICEIC
brief_extract: To assist Approved Contractors in interpreting these new regulations, the NICEIC, in co-operation with other bodies, has issued and published a 'Contractor's Handbook'. Over 38,000 copies of this publication have been distributed and sold, and applications for copies have come from as far afield as Hong Kong, Malaya and Africa. Quality and Reliability is the keynote; the sole criterion to acceptance as an Approved Electrical Contractor is the ability to do a good job.

The Domestic Appliances Division Information Centre, BEAMA, 8 Leicester Street, London, W.C.2., has a list of the names and addresses of manufacturers' service departments, approximate costs and suggested methods of packing and labelling to ensure safe delivery and safe return. THE NATIONAL INSPECTION COUNCIL FOR ELECTRICAL INSTALLATION CONTRACTING
Trafalgar Buildings, 1 Charing Cross, London, S.W.1
Telephone: Trafalgar 3723

BE ASSURED OF
QUALITY & RELIABILITY BY LOOKING FOR THIS SIGN
Approved Contractors on the Roll of the NICEIC voluntarily engage themselves to work to the standard of the IEE Wiring Regulations - 'the minimum requirements for safety from fire and shock' - and they are periodically inspected by the Council's engineers to ensure they maintain this standard. NATIONAL INSPECTION COUNCIL FOR ELECTRICAL INSTALLATION CONTRACTING
NICEIC

QR YEAR
OCTOBER 1966 - OCTOBER 1967

Your branch secretary or your nearest Electricity Showroom will show you a copy of the Council's Roll, from which you may make your choice.

brief_context: Country where Dutch hostesses will offer hospitality to EAW visitors.
brief_extract: Vos-Warnecke, the President of the NVEV, and Mrs. Ouwehand-Hartree attended our last Annual General Meeting in London they met many EAW members who recalled pleasant memories of their visits to Holland, asked after friends they had made during the special tour which was organised to Holland in 1964, or spoke of trips which they were planning for the future. Inspired by these talks our Dutch friends have evolved a hospitality plan which they hope will find as much favour with us as it is finding with them.

brief_context: Country where some EAW guests will travel from.
brief_extract: The Dutch have emphasised to their members that no one should be put off because she cannot offer lavish or extended hospitality or because she has not a great knowledge of the English language. So enthusiastic, however, is one Dutch branch about the idea that some of the members have offered to receive guests from Britain for a weekend or longer. This branch has even got an English conversation circle to which it hopes to invite EAW visitors.

brief_context: Mentioned as a destination for Dutch members to visit.
brief_extract: The scheme was developed further by another branch whose secretary suggested an exchange arrangement. She said she had always wanted to visit England but as her English was not fluent she had not had the courage to go alone. If, however, she could get to know someone from England by having her as a guest in her own home, she would then love to have the opportunity of paying a return visit.

brief_context: Region where an EAW area meeting was held.
brief_extract: We at EAW Headquarters most warmly welcome this initiative on the part of our Dutch friends and we are sure that there will be many EAW members who will wish to take part in the scheme either as guests or hostesses. When I broached the idea recently to an area meeting in the North East the response was enthusiastic and the immediate comment was: 'Why didn't we think of it first?'. Further details of the scheme will be announced as soon as possible but in the meantime I shall be glad to hear from any EAW members who would like to offer hospitality to Dutch visitors so that we can start compiling our list.

Some Glimpses of Expo 67

by PATRICIA HEDLEY, Editor of Housecraft

'MAN and his world' was the theme of Expo 67 — an exhibition of contrasts which must have made its many millions of visitors think harder about the differences between the developed and the underdeveloped countries, between what is and what could be. But mainly it struck an optimistic note, making one aware of the great potential of man's knowledge, of his originality as a designer and creator, of his ability to control and use resources.

brief_extract:

This was the first visit of the newly formed Branch and provided an enlightening glimpse into the use of electricity in industry. None of the members had imagined that the amount of electricity used to run the plant was sufficient to supply a town approximately the size of Bolton, and that it was purchased from the National Grid, nor were they prepared for the speed with which the huge presses turned out steel parts for car bodies; the spectacular display of spot welding and the unique method of inserting windscreens in seconds by the skilled use of a rubber hammer and length of string.

article_title: VISIT TO FORD MOTOR COMPANY, LIVERPOOL
brief_extract:
Hancock, Magazine Secretary, Heswall

This was the first visit of the newly formed Branch and provided an enlightening glimpse into the use of electricity in industry. None of the members had imagined that the amount of electricity used to run the plant was sufficient to supply a town approximately the size of Bolton, and that it was purchased from the National Grid, nor were they prepared for the speed with which the huge presses turned out steel parts for car bodies; the spectacular display of spot welding and the unique method of inserting windscreens in seconds by the skilled use of a rubber hammer and length of string. Members learned that of the 11,000 employees only 350 are women, all employed on the electrically
operated sewing machines for upholstery; a new American machine has been installed recently and sews at the rate of 30,000 stitches a minute.

C. Rees-Davies, Press Officer, Wallasey

On arrival members were given information about the computer and relevant equipment. They were then taken to see two punch card operators at work, one punching out the data off the meter readers' book, and the second one repunching the same card from the same book.
